title: Quantum Leakage Resilience of Shamir Secret Sharing
authors: Rishabh Batra, Fuyuki Kitagawa, Ryo Nishimaki, Takashi Yamakawa
abstract: We initiate the study of quantum leakage resilience of unmodified Shamir secret sharing over prime fields. A well-studied leakage model for Shamir's secret sharing classically is single-bit local leakage from each share. We consider its quantum analogue where, for each party, a local leakage channel takes as input the party's share and outputs a leaked qubit. Without preshared entanglement, we show that the distinguishing advantage is $2^{-Ω(n)}$ when the threshold rate $t/n=τ$ exceeds $τ_\star\approx0.73339$ by a fixed positive margin.   More generally, we allow disjoint entangled blocks of any fixed maximum size where there is no entanglement between different blocks or with the adversary, and each block emits at most a fixed number of qubits. Security holds when the threshold rate is high enough (sufficiently close to one). We then allow a specified set of devices to share entanglement with the adversary. We show that security holds even when a linear number of devices ($αn$ for small $α>0$) share entanglement with each other and with the adversary for a large enough threshold rate.   As a complementary negative result, we also show that even classical single-bit leakage makes Shamir scheme insecure if we allow arbitrarily large entanglement between the leakage devices. A GHZ state shared by exactly $t$ leakage devices makes even classical one-bit leakage insecure, without any entanglement with the adversary. In this attack, each participating device emits only one classical bit, and their joint parity distinguishes any chosen pair of secrets with a constant advantage. Thus, for fixed threshold rates above $τ_\star$, the maximum number of devices that may share arbitrary entanglement with one another and with the adversary while preserving security is linear in $n$ up to constant factors, although the optimal support fraction remains open.
summary: This work analyzes the security of Shamir's secret sharing scheme against quantum leakage attacks. Using advanced Fourier analysis on finite fields, the authors derive critical threshold rates required to ensure that the leaked quantum information is insufficient for an adversary to distinguish between possible secrets. The findings establish quantitative limits on the resilience of secret sharing in the presence of quantum side channels.
main_problem: The paper investigates the quantum leakage resilience of Shamir's secret sharing scheme, analyzing how easily an adversary can distinguish between two secrets based on leaked quantum information.
main_result: Security is maintained if the threshold rate $t/n$ exceeds a critical threshold $	au^\star \approx 0.73339$ when no entanglement is shared, and security can be extended to linear entanglement support under high threshold rates.
method: The analysis employs finite-field Fourier analysis, bounding the distinguishing advantage using properties of the dual MDS code and techniques like the MDS Brascamp-Lieb inequality.
model_or_system: The model is Shamir's secret sharing over prime fields, where the leakage is modeled as a local quantum channel outputting qubits from each share.
key_observables: Distinguishing advantage ($	ext{Adv}$), threshold rate ($	au = t/n$), and the critical threshold ($	au^\star$).
important_parameters: Threshold rate $	au$, field size $p$, and the entanglement support size ($\alpha n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the structure of the dual MDS code and relies on bounding the Fourier coefficients of the leakage operators.
figures_summary: The notes mention tables summarizing sufficient thresholds for different block sizes and theorems relating to the security bounds.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the basic quantum leakage bound without entanglement, then generalizing to disjoint entangled blocks, and finally analyzing the case where a linear number of devices share entanglement with the adversary.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous, information-theoretic bounds on the security of cryptographic primitives (secret sharing) against sophisticated quantum side-channel attacks, which is fundamental to quantum information security.
